title: Depth, initial gain, optimizers and residual blocks: four faces of one differential equation
summary: Gradient flow through a deep network is a product of layer factors; gradient descent is forward Euler on a gradient flow; momentum is a damped second-order ODE; and a stack of residual blocks is a numerical integrator in depth. These figures show each of these statements at work.

media.alt: Three panels. Left, titled gradient flow against depth (tanh, width 100): first-layer weight gradient norm on a log axis from 1e-15 to 1e3 against depth from 2 to 64 hidden layers, one curve per initial gain from 0.6 (purple, falling by twelve decades) to 2.0 (yellow, rising). Middle, a 3D surface over depth and gain. Right, titled vanishing below gain 1, growing above: log of growth per layer against initial gain, with measured points and a mean-field dashed curve through them, crossing zero at gain 1.

read_the_figure.question: Does the learning signal survive the depth of this network at this initialization, and which optimizer or integrator choice is stable at this step?
read_the_figure.axes: Gain figures: depth (hidden layers, log) or initial gain against the first-layer gradient norm (log) or the log growth per layer. Optimizer figures: iteration against loss ratio (log), or learning rate times maximum curvature, or momentum and step on the stability map. Residual figures: number of blocks N against error (log) or cost, and Jacobian norm against N.
look_at: Gradient against depth: at gain 0.6 the first-layer gradient falls roughly twelve decades from depth 2 to 64; at gain 1.0 it is nearly flat; above 1 it grows. The animation still (gain 0.90, 40 layers) prints that the first-layer gradient is 0.0051 of the last.
Growth per layer against gain: the measured dots follow the mean-field curve and cross zero at gain 1, the critical initialization.

GD as Euler: the iteration count to 1e-6 falls as the step eta times L_max approaches the Euler limit 2 (dashed line); the best fixed step is 2/(mu + L). The heavy-ball map shows a stability edge in the (alpha L, beta) plane with the optimum marked.
Race on a quadratic with condition number 100: plain GD needs several hundred iterations, heavy ball and Nesterov about a hundred, RMSprop and Adam sit between.
Race on a small tanh network: five optimizers with best learning rates; the legend gives their final losses; Adam is lowest with periodic spikes, SGD has two large spikes.

Effective weight decay: with Adam plus L2 each weight loses a different fraction per step (a broad histogram); decoupled weight decay (AdamW) removes the same fraction from every weight (a single line); a ridge penalty on rescaled features changes the predictions unless the penalty is rescaled by 1 over a squared.

Residual blocks: Euler-type blocks give error falling with slope -1 against depth, RK4-type blocks slope -4.1; against cost RK4 blocks win by many decades; the unit-step stack has a Jacobian norm that grows with depth while a step scaled by 1/N stays bounded.
read_the_figure.proves: Depth, gain and step size interact multiplicatively: a gain of 0.9 over 40 layers loses a factor of 200, a step above 2/L makes gradient descent diverge, and a residual stack with the step 1/N is a convergent integrator in depth with the order of the block's rule.
if_wrong: Gradient norm falling exponentially with depth: gain below 1 (vanishing) or saturation.
A learning rate times curvature above 2: explicit gradient descent diverges.
Different effective decay per weight under Adam plus L2: the penalty is not what a ridge penalty promises.
A residual stack with unit steps and growing Jacobian: the continuous-depth limit is not reached.
must_check: That the log axis and the layer width are stated.
That the optimizer comparison states the learning-rate grid and the budget.
That the stability bound for the step size is marked on the plot.
That the residual stack's step size is scaled with depth.

terms.meaning: The scale of the random initial weights times the square root of fan-in; gain 1 keeps signals at constant size.
The ODE of steepest descent in continuous time.
Gradient descent with momentum; a damped second-order ODE in continuous time.
h_{k+1} = h_k + (1/N) f(h_k): one Euler step of an ODE in depth.
A shrink of the weights by a fixed fraction independent of the gradient scaling (AdamW).

remember: Backpropagated gradient norms scale like (gain times slope)^depth.
Gradient descent with step eta is stable on a quadratic if eta L_max < 2.
Momentum allows a larger step: heavy ball reaches rate (sqrt(kappa)-1)/(sqrt(kappa)+1).
Adam's L2 penalty is rescaled per weight by the gradient statistics; AdamW's decay is not.
A residual stack with N blocks and step 1/N converges as N grows with the order of its block rule.

steps.title: Gradient through depth
steps.note: At gain 0.9 and 40 layers the animation's ratio 0.0051 means g times s of about 0.876 per layer (computed: 0.0051^(1/40)); gain below 1 vanishes and above 1 explodes.

steps.title: Gradient descent as forward Euler
steps.note: The Euler stability limit of the earlier figures, applied to the curvature. The dashed line at 2 in the first panel is this limit, and the best fixed step 2/(mu + L) balances the slowest and fastest modes.

steps.title: Residual blocks as Euler steps
steps.note: The depth axis is time. The fitted slopes -0.99 and -4.11 are the orders of the two rules, exactly as for explicit solvers in time.

steps.title: Equivalence of a penalty under feature scaling
steps.note: Rescaling a feature by a changes a ridge penalty into a generalized one with weight 1 over a squared; the figure's difference of 1e-16 for the rescaled penalty and order one for the unscaled one is this fact.

worked.title: How much gradient survives 40 layers at gain 0.9
worked.problem: Assume a per-layer factor 0.876 (derived from the animation still). What fraction of the last-layer gradient reaches the first layer after 40 layers? Compare with the printed 0.0051.
worked.answer: About 0.005, matching the printed 0.0051 (the factor was derived from it); with gain exactly 0.9 and a typical tanh slope below one the factor is a little below 0.9.

analyze.q: All curves in the first panel start within about a decade of each other at depth 2 and fan out with depth. Why?
analyze.hint: The gain compounds layer by layer.

analyze.q: Why is the limit eta L_max = 2 shown as a dashed line on the iteration-count panel?
Explain why AdamW's decay appears as a single vertical line in the weights histogram.

checks.hint: Where growth per layer is zero.
checks.answer: Gain 1: signals and gradients keep their size across layers.

checks.q: Why does momentum allow a larger step?
checks.answer: It acts as a damped second-order system whose stability region in (alpha, beta) is larger than the Euler limit for plain steps.

checks.q: The residual stack with unit steps has a Jacobian that grows with depth. Is it still a Neural ODE?
checks.answer: Only if the step is scaled with depth; with unit steps it is a different discrete map with no continuous-depth limit.

checks.q: Design a diagnostic that tells at initialization whether the gradient will vanish.
checks.answer: Measure the norm of the backpropagated gradient layer by layer for a random batch and plot it on a log axis; a straight line with negative slope means vanishing.
